text: High Level Data Flow

1. Account access: customers register or log in through Authentication, and their identifiers link to users records. Staff login additionally requires an active staffAccounts record. Administrators provision staff through the protected backend.

2. Branch and order entry: customers read branch information and prices, select a branch, provide laundry details and priority, and confirm the estimate. The order stores its customer and branch identifiers and starts as pending_dropoff.

3. Physical intake: staff at the selected branch inspect the laundry and enter verified quantities and the final price. The estimate remains available for comparison. Acceptance of the laundry changes the order to received.

4. Processing and alerts: staff change the order to washing, drying, and ready as work progresses. The ready transition creates a notification event and triggers a push attempt. The customer reads only their own status and notification records.

5. Settlement and history: at collection, staff verify and record the in-person payment. A protected operation checks the ready notification, payment, and pickup confirmation before changing the order to completed. Completed orders appear in customer history.

6. Administration: the administrator maintains branch information and prices, manages staff access, and monitors operations. Staff account actions retain creator and timestamp information. Passwords never enter Firestore or audit logs.
2.2 Design
User Interface Design

The interface uses consistent navigation, readable labels, clear progress states, and visible validation. Order details identify the branch and distinguish estimated from final prices. Confirmation views explain the effect of intake verification, cancellation, payment recording, and completion. Loading, empty, and failed-network states provide a clear next action.

Customer screens comprise sign up/login, profile, branch dashboard, branch details and map, order entry, estimate confirmation, active order details, notifications, and completed history. A progress indicator explains pending drop-off, received, washing, drying, ready, and completed using ordinary language.

Staff screens comprise login, the working-branch queue, laundry verification, processing details, ready orders, payment entry, and completion confirmation. The branch identifier is visible. Payment is recorded at collection after readiness notification and shows the final amount and responsible staff member.

Administrator screens comprise login, dashboard, staff creation, staff access control, branch/pricing management, and monitoring. The staff creation form contains only email and temporary password. Role, creator, creation time, and active status are assigned automatically. Password input is masked and never displayed again after creation.
Database Design

Firestore collections and documents provide the logical equivalent of tables and records. Document identifiers are primary keys, while identifier fields connect related records. The proposed schema follows the updated workflow; rules and trusted operations enforce relationships and permissions.

text: One customer has many orders, and one branch has many orders; each order belongs to one customer and one branch. Staff identifiers connect verification, status changes, and payments to accountable users. An order has zero or one verified settlement payment in this scope and may have multiple notifications. Each notification belongs to a customer and an order. Authentication identifiers match the corresponding profile document identifiers.

Money is stored in integer minor units, such as centavos, to prevent rounding drift. Server timestamps establish the audit sequence. A pricing snapshot preserves the basis of an existing charge when branch prices change. Trusted logic checks customer-supplied quantities and recalculates estimates and final totals.

Branch assignment is a separate administrator-controlled action after staff account creation. It does not add inputs to the required email-and-temporary-password form. New staff receive no branch write access until assigned. The initial administrator is provisioned through trusted administrative setup.

The application uses Firebase SDK authentication and permitted Firestore reads under security rules. The following proposed callable functions define backend contracts; they are specifications, not a claim of deployed services. The logical endpoint is POST /{functionName} at the configured regional function host. Callable requests use a data object and successful responses use a result object; the SDK handles this envelope and attaches the Firebase identity token.

The response contains an order identifier, pending_dropoff status, and server-calculated estimate. These values illustrate the contract only.

Structured error codes include unauthenticated, permission-denied, invalid-argument, not-found, failed-precondition, and already-exists. The app shows useful messages without internal details. Request identifiers make retries safe; transactions prevent duplicate settlement. A push failure does not undo ready status: the notification remains available in the app and its delivery can be retried.

Read operations include own customer profile, branches, own orders/notifications, the authorized staff branch queue, and administrator monitoring. Queries must match security rules and use indexes and pagination. Public access must not expose passwords, unrestricted customer records, or role administration.
2.3 Development Process
Development Methodology

The project will use iterative development. Each iteration selects approved requirements, designs the interface and data changes, implements the feature, tests it, and presents a demonstration for review. Feedback updates the backlog. Requirements and the workflow serve as the acceptance basis.

The first iteration covers authentication, roles, and branches; the second covers estimates, ordering, and intake; the third covers status updates, ready alerts, and settlement. The final iteration integrates the system, resolves defects, evaluates security and usability, and prepares release and support materials.
Development Timeline

X indicates planned activity. Week 1 begins on the approved start date. This eight-week baseline covers the full cycle and does not represent completed work. At each weekly review, the team will update actual dates, progress, dependencies, and revised release expectations.
Version Control and Branching Strategy

The team will use a shared Git repository. The main branch contains reviewed, releasable work; a development branch integrates accepted features. Short-lived feature and fix branches address individual requirements or defects. Descriptive commits and pull requests reference issue identifiers, and release tags identify the exact application, rules, and backend versions deployed.

Credentials, service account keys, customer exports, and generated builds must not be committed. Configuration examples document variable names without secret values. The lockfile is retained for repeatable dependencies, and schema/rule changes are reviewed alongside affected code.
Code Review Procedures

Each pull request states the change, linked requirement, validation, and relevant screenshots. Another team member reviews correctness, role and branch restrictions, error handling, maintainability, and user behavior. Checks and review comments must be resolved before merging. The author updates affected documentation and test cases.
CHAPTER 3
TESTING DEPLOYMENT AND MAINTENANCE
3.1 Testing
Testing Strategy

Testing will combine unit tests for calculations and validation; integration tests for Authentication, Firestore, and backend operations; security-rule tests; and complete workflow tests. Manual device checks cover readability, permissions, network interruption, and notifications. Regression tests verify affected core scenarios after changes.

A dedicated test environment will contain separate customers, an administrator, active/inactive staff, at least two branches, and every order state. Each execution records version, device, network conditions, inputs, actual result, evidence, and pass/fail status. text: Bug Tracking and Issue Management

A shared issue tracker records identifier, summary, reporter, affected version/environment, reproduction steps, expected/actual behavior, evidence, severity, owner, and status. Issues move through Open, Assigned, In Progress, Ready for Retest, and Closed; failed retests reopen the issue.

Unauthorized access, lost orders, and incorrect or duplicate payment records are critical and block release. Other issues are prioritized by workflow impact and client agreement. Closure requires retest evidence and a regression check where relevant. Screenshots and logs exclude unnecessary personal data; known limitations appear in release notes.
3.2 Deployment
Deployment Steps

1. Prepare the release candidate: freeze approved scope, resolve blocking defects, complete required tests, and record the release tag, dependency versions, rules, indexes, functions, and configuration.

2. Configure the target environment: confirm the Firebase project, Authentication settings, Firestore rules/indexes, trusted backend, notification credentials, and map configuration. Provision the administrator securely, validate branch data, and authorize staff assignments.

3. Back up and deploy to staging: retain the previous release and configuration and back up data before risky changes. Deploy compatible rules, indexes, and backend functions, then produce the Expo mobile test build.

4. Run staging verification and user acceptance: exercise all roles and the complete workflow, security boundaries, notifications, retries, and payment reconciliation. Fix blocking issues, train client representatives, and record their actual acceptance decision.

5. Release through the agreed distribution channel: publish the approved build or authorized installation package with its compatible backend configuration. Retain the previous working release and the recovery instructions.

6. Verify after release: check login, branches, order creation, processing updates, ready alerts, settlement, and history. Monitor errors, record deployment results, and provide release notes and support guidance.

Rollback Procedures

The release owner initiates rollback for security failures, inconsistent orders/payments, widespread crashes, or broken critical workflows. Restrict affected writes when necessary, preserve logs and a current snapshot, and inform the client representative.

Restore the last verified compatible application and backend configuration. Prefer backward-compatible schema changes. Restore data only after evaluating transactions created since the backup; reconcile recent orders/payments rather than overwriting valid activity blindly. Retest critical scenarios before resuming full access and document the incident and corrective action.

3.3 Maintenance
Maintenance and Support Plan

During the agreed support period, a designated maintenance owner will monitor authentication/application errors, failed alerts, and order/payment consistency. Critical security and payment incidents receive immediate triage; routine defects and improvements enter the backlog. The client and team will agree on support coverage and response commitments at handover.

Weekly reviews examine open issues, failed notifications, staff/branch access, and backup results. Monthly reviews assess dependencies, device compatibility, recurring errors, and documentation. Changes affecting roles, rules, calculations, data structures, or state transitions require staging validation and a recovery plan.

The administrator deactivates departing staff promptly while preserving history. Backups follow the agreed schedule, and restoration exercises verify usability. Diagnostics collect only information needed to resolve an issue.
Documentation Updates

Accepted changes update the requirements, screen descriptions, schema, API contracts, tests, deployment procedures, and user guide. Release notes identify version, date, changes, known issues, and operator actions. Approved documentation is stored with the corresponding release, while prior versions remain traceable.
User Support Channels and Resources

Customers use an in-app help/FAQ resource and the branch's published contact details. Staff report operational problems to the administrator, who escalates application defects to the designated development support contact. Reports include order identifier, time, device, and description, but never a password.

Handover resources include customer/staff guides, administrator access instructions, troubleshooting and recovery guides, release notes, and agreed support contacts. Training demonstrates the complete workflow, estimates versus final prices, failed notifications, and disputed records.
CONCLUSION
Summary

WashWise is proposed to coordinate branch selection, laundry orders, staff verification, processing visibility, ready notifications, and recorded in-person settlement. Customers physically drop off and collect laundry. Administrators control staff access, branches, and pricing; authorized staff handle branch operations.

The requirements and plans provide an implementation and evaluation basis. Benefits must be established through actual testing and client use. Release readiness requires verified workflow behavior, access controls, payment consistency, and client acceptance.
Future Work

Future improvements may include operational reporting, completion estimates informed by recorded workload, accessibility refinements, and broader device support. Additional services require separate scope approval, revised design, and acceptance tests.
